The BrainAmp plugin streams Brain Products BrainAmp amplifiers into MNE Scan through the brainamp:// source of the mne_acq_devices library. Without an amplifier it simulates one.

The plugin is built by default. To talk to a real amplifier on Windows, copy BrainAmpIoCtl.h from the BrainAmp SDK into src/apps/mne_scan/plugins/brainamp, or point CMake at the directory that holds it: cmake -B build -DMNE_BRAINAMP_SDK_DIR=C:/BrainAmpSDK Without the header the source only simulates.

Install the BrainAmp USB driver from the software that came with the amplifier and switch the amplifier on before starting MNE Scan. The setup widget sets Channels: EEG channels, 32 per amplifier and up to 128. The amplifiers must be connected in order. Resolution: the step of one bit, 100 nV, 500 nV, 10 µV or 152.6 µV. Samples per block: samples handed to the connected plugins at once. Simulate the amplifier: streams the amplifier's wire format with synthetic EEG and trigger codes. The amplifier samples at 5000 Hz. The marker word arrives as the stimulus channel STI 014.

The same source is available to every program that links mne_acq_devices: #include <mne/acq/acq_device.h> #include <mne/acq/devices/acq_devices.h> mne::registerBrainAmpScheme(); auto device = mne::AcqDevice::open("brainamp://?simulate=1&channels=64&resolution=500nV"); simulate=1 also accepts seed, realtime=0 (as fast as possible), duration in seconds and gain.

The BrainFlow plugin streams any board BrainFlow supports (OpenBCI Cyton and Ganglion, g.tec Unicorn, Muse, ANT Neuro eego, the synthetic board, ...). MNE-CPP does not ship BrainFlow: it uses an installed BrainFlow 5 at run time, found in this order: the path entered as BrainFlow library, the environment variable MNE_CPP_BRAINFLOW_LIB (path of BoardController), the library of the Python package, after pip install brainflow, the system library paths. Follow the steps below to stream a board: Install BrainFlow, e.g. pip install brainflow. Start MNE Scan and add the BrainFlow plugin. Enter the Board: a BrainFlow board id (-1) or name (synthetic, cyton_daisy, CYTON_DAISY_BOARD). synthetic needs no hardware. Enter the BrainFlow input parameters the board needs, as in BrainFlow's documentation: e.g. Serial port for a Cyton (/dev/ttyUSB0, COM3), MAC address for a Muse, IP address and IP port for WiFi boards. Start the pipeline. Every row of the board becomes a channel: EEG, EMG, ECG and EOG in volts (BrainFlow reports microvolts), the accelerometer, gyroscope and other rows as BrainFlow delivers them, the timestamp row in seconds and the marker row as a trigger channel. A board that this platform's BrainFlow does not include, or another BrainFlow version than 5, is refused with the reason in the log. The plugin reads the board through the brainflow:// source of the acquisition library, so the same board opens with mne_acq, e.g. mne_acq view "brainflow://cyton?serial_port=/dev/ttyUSB0".
The EEGoSports plugin streams ANT Neuro eego amplifiers into MNE Scan through the eego:// source of the mne_acq_devices library. Without an amplifier it simulates one.

The plugin is built by default. At run time the source loads the eego SDK library (eego-SDK.dll on Windows, libeego-SDK.so on Linux), which ANT Neuro ships with the amplifier, from the path in the environment variable MNE_CPP_EEGO_SDK or else through the system loader. Switch the amplifier on before starting the acquisition. The setup widget sets Sampling frequency: one of the amplifier's rates, 512 Hz by default. Block size: the samples per block handed to the connected plugins. Simulate the amplifier: 64 referential and 24 bipolar inputs that stream synthetic EEG and trigger codes in the SDK's format. The referential inputs are named and placed after the electrodes of the cap layout chosen in the project setup, which also sets the cardinal points: tracked ones from their own .elc file, or electrodes of the cap lowered by a given distance. The bipolar inputs are BIP 1 onwards, the trigger input STI 014, and the amplifier's sample counter COUNTER. The Check impedance values action measures the electrode impedances, also of the simulated amplifier.

The same source is available to every program that links mne_acq_devices: #include <mne/acq/acq_device.h> #include <mne/acq/devices/acq_devices.h> mne::register_eego_scheme(); auto device = mne::AcqDevice::open("eego://?simulate=1&reference=32&bipolar=0&rate=1000"); auto impedances = device->measureImpedances(); The target selects an amplifier by serial number (eego://000123); sdk= gives the SDK library's path, and reference_range and bipolar_range the input ranges in volts. simulate=1 also accepts seed, realtime=0 (as fast as possible), duration in seconds and gain.

The forward solution plugin handles all forward computation tasks within MNE Scan. It can be used to compute the EEG and MEG forward solution, based on a BEM and source model. Further, it is possible to update the MEG forward solution to a new head position provided by the HPI Fitting plugin.
The Forward Solution plugin takes data from following plugins: Sensor Plugins: FiffSimulator plugin, FieldTripBuffer plugin HPI Fitting plugin
The computed forward solution can be passed to the Source Localization plugin.

Load the Forward Solution Plugin from the Algorithm Plugins available in MNE Scan To compute the forward solution within MNE Scan, some files and settings have to be loaded respectively set before the start of the measurement. They can be accessed by clicking on the Forward Solution plugin in the Plugin Scene. | Please note: The measurement file can be an arbitrary measurement file observed on the System of choice. It is only used to extract the system-specific compensator data.| If not specified, the BEM model defaults to a sphere model.

Once the settings are specified, and the aspired pipeline is designed, the measurement can be started. Open the control widget. Navigate to the Forward Solution tab. | Please note: If connected to the HPI Fitting plugin, the Forward Solution control widget first appears after the first successful HPI fit.| Compute the forward solution by pressing Compute Forward Solution. To pass the forward solution to the Source Localization plugin, it is necessary to enable the checkbox Cluster Forward Solution. If connected to the HPI Fitting plugin, it is possible to activate Enable head position update to update the forward solution once the defined thresholds within the HPI Plugin are exceeded. | Please note: This is not yet real-time capable. The forward solution computation takes some seconds. Therefore it is wise to choose the thresholds not too small.|

In the following picture, some examples for processing pipelines, including the Forward Solution plugins, are presented. The pipeline on the left represents an easy source localization pipeline, whereas the right one can be used to compensate head movements during the measurement. The current head position, estimated by the HPI Fitting plugin, is used to update and recompute the forward solution. For this pipeline, it is further necessary to filter out the cHPI data before averaging. For further guides on setting up the components see: HPI Fitting plugin Source Localization plugin.

The FtBuffer plugin reads a FieldTrip buffer server through the ftbuffer:// source of the mne_acq_devices library. It is only a client: it reads what a producer puts into the buffer and has no access to the device itself. Without a server it simulates neuromag2ft on a Neuromag system. The setup widget sets Host and Port of the buffer server (default localhost and 1972). Samples per block: the block size handed to the connected plugins. Simulate neuromag2ft and its buffer: a 306-channel Neuromag system relayed into a simulated buffer. On start the plugin waits for the producer's header and then streams the samples put after that moment. With the Neuromag header of neuromag2ft, the channels, their coil types and positions, the measurement info and the digitizer points of the acquisition are used, the samples are already in tesla and volts, and changes of STI 014 (or STI101) become events. Other producers give the channel names of their header, or numbered channels. Events put into the buffer with a numeric value become events with that code. When the producer puts a new header, i.e. starts a new measurement, the stream ends; start the plugin again.

Download FieldTrip neuromag2ft Download the FieldTrip source code on your acquisition computer, either from their website or their GitHub page. The executable neuromag2ft both hosts the buffer and puts the acquisition's data into it. Get neuromag2ft set up Depending on your system, you might have to build it locally with make in /realtime/src/acquisition/neuromag/. If in doubt, follow the documentation of the FieldTrip buffer. Run neuromag2ft Run neuromag2ft on the acquisition computer before the measurement starts; --help lists its options. By default the buffer listens on port 1972. Set up the plugin in MNE Scan Select the FtBuffer plugin, enter the address of the acquisition computer and the port, and start MNE Scan. The Neuromag plugin reads the acquisition directly, without neuromag2ft, but runs on the acquisition computer itself.

The same source is available to every program that links mne_acq_devices: #include <mne/acq/acq_device.h> #include <mne/acq/devices/acq_devices.h> mne::register_ftbuffer_scheme(); auto device = mne::AcqDevice::open("ftbuffer://megacq:1972"); timeout is how long to wait for the connection and the producer's header. ftbuffer://?simulate=1 accepts meg, eeg, rate, block (samples per put), seed, realtime=0 (as fast as possible) and duration in seconds.
The GUSBAmp plugin streams up to four synchronised g.tec g.USBamp amplifiers into MNE Scan through the gusbamp:// source of the mne_acq_devices library. Without amplifiers it simulates them.

The plugin is built by default. On Windows it loads the g.USBamp API (gUSBamp.dll) from the system directory at run time; the amplifier's USB driver installs it there. Connect the units with the synchronisation cable and switch them on before starting the acquisition. The setup widget sets Serial numbers: the units, separated by commas, master first (e.g. UB-2015.05.16,UB-2015.05.17); empty for the first connected unit. Inputs: the inputs 1 to 16 acquired on every unit, e.g. 1-8,11. Sample rate: 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 600, 1200, 2400, 4800, 9600, 19200 or 38400 Hz. Samples per block: the block size handed to the connected plugins. Trigger line: the master's trigger input as STI 014; its changes become events. Simulate the amplifiers: synthetic EEG and trigger codes in the API's format, for the given serial numbers. The channels are EEG 001 onwards, the inputs of the master first, then those of each slave. The amplifiers run without their hardware filters, unipolar, with no common reference or ground.

The same source is available to every program that links mne_acq_devices: #include <mne/acq/acq_device.h> #include <mne/acq/devices/acq_devices.h> mne::register_gusbamp_scheme(); auto device = mne::AcqDevice::open("gusbamp://UB-1,UB-2?simulate=1&inputs=1-8&rate=512&trigger=1"); auto impedances = device->measureImpedances(); simulate=1 also accepts seed, realtime=0 (as fast as possible), duration in seconds and gain.

This guide shows how to enable and use real-time head monitoring during a MEG measurement. Currently, only Neuromag/Elekta/MEGIN devices are supported. Method · API · Example Continuous head position (cHPI) Fitting of head-position indicator coils during the recording to track and compensate head movement. Understand the method Real-time Head Monitoring Use the API InvHpiFit Run an example Estimate the head position from HPI coilsStart here Fit continuous HPI coils Real-time averaging, covariance and inverse workers

Before you can monitor head movements during a measurement, ensur eyou have the following things setup: Enable continuous HPI (cHPi) during your measurement. Make sure you have digitized the subjects head (fiducials, HPI coils and additional head points) and you have access to the data.

Real-time head monitoring works in combination with sensor plugins, such as the FiffSimulator or FieldTripBuffer. The following steps guide you through setting up the real-time head monitoring in MNE Scan: Setup the data stream. You can either: Stream pre-recorded data via the FiffSimulator plugin. Stream data from a MEG device connected via the FieldTripBuffer plugin. Add the HPI Fitting plugin to the plugin scene and connect your sensor plugin from step one to the HPI Plugin. Start the measurement via the Play button in the top left corner You can open and control the settings for the HPI fitting via the Quick Control View. Open it by pressing the QUICK CTRL button and follow the steps described in the next section. MNE Scan should now look like following picture. You have the plugin scene on the left, the 3D View in the upper part and the data stream in the lower part. The 3D View shows an average head model that is aligned and scaled to digitized landmarks like LPA, RPA, Nasion and HPI coils. The head moddel shows up after the first succesfull HPI fit.

The Quick Control View can be used to choose between different tabs, where every tab correspondds to one plugin. In case of a basic HPI Fitting pipeline, there should be three tabs: FiffSimulator or FieldTripBuffer, HpI Fitting and 3D View. The HPI Fitting and 3D View tabs and their functionalities are described in the following:

The control widget for the HPI Fitting plugin consist of three tabs: Load Digitizer, Fitting and Head Movements. Load Digitizer​ Click the button Load Digitizers and navigate to the subject's digitized data which is stored in .fif format. The display will show how many digitizers of each kind were loaded. Enter the HPI coil frequencies. You can add and remove frequencies. If you don't know how your coils and frequencies are ordered, do an initial frequency ordering by pressing Order coil frequencies. Fitting​ Choose if you want to use Signal Space Projection (SSP) or Compensators when performing the fit. Do an initial HPI fit or enable continuous HPI fitting. Make sure you have started the measuring pipeline via the play button first. After the first succesfull fit the average head should appear in the 3D View. The Fitting errors are shown in mm for each coil and as an average over all coils. The error is calculated as the distance between the estimated HPI coils and the digitized HPI positions. Choose a threshold that defines an acceptable error. Head Movements​ Choose a threshold that defines big head movements by rotation (degree) and movement (mm). Once exceeded, e.g., the forward solution recomputation is triggered.

Here you can choose what elements you want to visualize in the monitoring section. These elements include: Device > VectorView or BabyMEG features the helmet surfaces for different MEG devices. Head > Average, Tracked and Fitted features the averaged head surface, digitized and aligned landmarks as well as the estimated HPI coil locations, respectivley.
The HPI Fitting Plugin can be connected to following Plugins: Input: FiffSimulator plugin, FieldTripBuffer plugin. Output: Forward Solution plugin
MNE Scan can send clips of recording data to MNE Analyze in real time. Follow this guide to set it up.

This plugin adds support for LSL data streams to MNE Scan. MNE-CPP includes a self-contained LSL library under src/libs/mne/lsl that implements the core LSL protocol (stream discovery via UDP multicast, data transport via TCP), eliminating the need for any external dependency. For more information about the original LSL project please see: LSL on Github

The LSL plugin is built by default. Configure the project as usual: cmake -B build -S . cmake --build build No external submodule or library is required — the built-in mne_lsl library provides all necessary LSL functionality.
Build MNE Scan. Start MNE Scan — the LSL adapter plugin will be available in the sensor plugins list.

|Please note: We are working with the SDK v 8.4 so we are only able to connect to a Quantum system. These are typically used in phase 2 surgery of epilepsy.| Follow the steps below to connect to a Natus amplifier: Select streaming machine. If not present add it to the SelectStreamingMachine Visual studio project and rebuild. Start the startDataTransmit.bat . Check if it connects and streams data based on the message in the left lower corner. Start MNE Scan and add the Natus plugin. Enter the number of channels and the sampling rate set on the amplifier; the datagrams carry the channel count, so a wrong one stops the stream with a message, but not the rate. The streaming machine sends to UDP port 50000 by default; set the address and port where MNE Scan receives them. Simulate the streaming machine streams a synthetic session without the amplifier. The plugin reads the amplifier through the natus:// source of the acquisition library, which works on every platform, e.g. mne_acq view "natus://0.0.0.0?port=50000&channels=46&rate=2048". The streaming machine sends its values in units of 0.1 µV; the source turns them into volts.

The Neuromag plugin streams a Neuromag / MEGIN (Elekta) Vectorview or TRIUX MEG system into MNE Scan through the neuromag:// source of the mne_acq_devices library. It reads the acquisition software (DACQ) directly, the way the Neuromag plugin of mne_rt_server did until 2020. Without a system it simulates one.

The plugin is built by default; reading a real system needs Linux or macOS, the simulator runs everywhere. MNE Scan runs on the acquisition workstation itself: the source registers as a client of the DACQ data server through its UNIX socket in <root>/sockets, receives the data buffers through the server's shared memory or files, and starts and stops measurements through the collector (TCP port 11122). The setup widget sets Acquisition directory: the DACQ root, /neuro/dacq by default. Samples per data buffer: the buffer length set on the collector before a measurement; as set up keeps it. Samples per block: the block size handed to the connected plugins. Start and stop the measurement: let the plugin start a measurement on the collector; clear it to follow measurements started from the acquisition user interface. Simulate the acquisition: 306 MEG channels and STI 014 at 1 kHz in the data server's format. The channels, their calibration, coil types and positions come from the measurement info the acquisition sends at the start of each measurement. The trigger channel is STI 014, otherwise STI101; its changes become events.

The FtBuffer plugin reads a FieldTrip buffer, which FieldTrip's neuromag2ft fills on the acquisition workstation; it runs on any computer on the network. The Neuromag plugin needs no further software but runs on the acquisition workstation.

The same source is available to every program that links mne_acq_devices: #include <mne/acq/acq_device.h> #include <mne/acq/devices/acq_devices.h> mne::register_neuromag_scheme(); auto device = mne::AcqDevice::open("neuromag://?simulate=1&meg=306&eeg=64&rate=1000"); host, port and client select the collector and the data server's client id; timeout is how long to wait for the measurement info. simulate=1 also accepts meg, eeg, rate, buffer, seed, realtime=0 (as fast as possible), duration in seconds and gain.

Follow these steps to playback recorded data through the MNE Rt Server to MNE Scan. Pass the path to the file you would like to stream via the -f or --file command line argument. For example: mne_rt_server --file ../resources/data/MNE-sample-data/MEG/sample/ernoise_raw.fif. Alternativley, you can navigate and edit to the FiffSimulation.cfg file manually. Open the mne-cpp\resources\mne_rt_server\plugins\fiffsimulator\FiffSimulation.cfg with a text editor and insert the path and file name of the fif file which you want to stream. For example: simFile = ../resources/data/MNE-sample-data/MEG/sample/ernoise_raw.fif Start the mne_rt_server mne-cpp\out\Release\apps\mne_rt_server Start MNE Scan mne-cpp\out\Release\apps\mne_scan Select the FiffSimulator plug-in and place it on the plug-in scene. Click on the FiffSimulator plug-in. Its settings are the host and command port of mne_rt_server (127.0.0.1 and 4217 for a server on your machine; the data port is the next one), the file the server replays (empty keeps the server's file) and the samples per block. We recommend a block size equal to the sampling frequency, so the display refreshes every second. Without a server, Simulate the server replays a synthetic Neuromag recording. The plug-in reads the server through the rtserver:// source of the acquisition library, e.g. mne_acq view "rtserver://127.0.0.1:4217?simfile=/data/run_raw.fif&buffer=1000" reads it the same way. Press the green play button in the left upper corner. If you click on the FiffSimulator plug-in you should now see the real-time data display.

This tutorial will show how you can set up an acquisition and real-time source localization pipeline in MNE Scan. Make sure you correctly setup the MNE Sample Data Set. On MacOS please make sure that you copied the MNE-Sample-data-set to mne_scan.app/Contents/MacOS/ as well. Start mne_rt_server in your mne-cpp/out/Release folder. Start mne_scan in your mne-cpp/out/Release folder. Navigate to the "Sensor Plugins" and "Algorithm Plugins" buttons in the plugin window. Select and position the following plugins onto the plugin scene: Sensor Plugins - FiffSimulator Algorithm Plugins - Averaging Algorithm Plugins - Forward Solution Algorithm Plugins - Covariance Algorithm Plugins - MNE Select the "Connection tool" in the plugin window. Connect the plugins as follows by left clicking on the start, holding and releasing above the target plugin. Start the pipeline via the green "Play" button in the top left corner. Now that you should see the different views for each plugin displaying the incoming data, averages and so on. Click on the Averaging plugin. Choose the correct trigger channel. For example STI014 when streaming the default file sample_audvis_raw.fif. Once the averages are starting to come in you can take a look at the averaged data in form of a butterfly and 2D layout plot. Click on the Forward Solution plugin. Make sure that the "Cluster forward solution" box is checked. Press the "Compute Forward Solution" button. Wait until the "Status computation" label shows a green Finished. Computing the forward solution may take some time. However, this only has to be done once. Once the forward solution was calculated, the source localization plugin controls should appear in the QuickControlView. Select the plugin. Choose the source localization method, trigger type and time point you want to visualize. If you set the time point outside the range of the computed average (e.g. 1000ms), the data will be streamed sample by sample. You can change the 3D visualization setting by selecting the "3D View" plugin controls in the QuickControlView. If you prefer cortically constrained interpolation you can switch from "Annotation based" to "Interpolation based". The threshold of the plotted activation can be changed by clicking on the field with the three floating values. This will open a histogram based thresholding widget. Use the left, middle and right mouse buttons to set the threshold values.
The TMSI plugin streams TMSi Refa and Porti amplifiers into MNE Scan through the tmsi:// source of the mne_acq_devices library. Without an amplifier it simulates one.

The plugin is built by default. On Windows it loads the TMSi SDK (TMSiSDK.dll, or TMSiSDK32bit.dll for a 32-bit build) from the system directory at run time; the amplifier's USB driver installs it there. Switch the amplifier on before starting the acquisition. The setup widget sets Sampling rate: the amplifier runs at the supported rate nearest to it, its base rate of 2048 Hz divided by 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16. Number of channels: the leading amplifier channels to deliver, or all. Use common average: reference the ExG inputs to their average in the amplifier. Simulate the amplifier: a Refa with 64 ExG inputs that streams synthetic EEG and trigger codes in the SDK's 32-bit format. Trigger beep and keyboard trigger: write codes 252 (beep), 254 (left) and 253 (right) into STI 014. The ExG inputs are named and placed after the electrodes of the cap layout chosen in the project setup. The Check impedance values action measures the electrode impedances, also of the simulated amplifier.

The same source is available to every program that links mne_acq_devices: #include <mne/acq/acq_device.h> #include <mne/acq/devices/acq_devices.h> mne::registerTmsiScheme(); auto device = mne::AcqDevice::open("tmsi://?simulate=1&exg=32&rate=1024"); auto impedances = device->measureImpedances(); simulate=1 also accepts seed, realtime=0 (as fast as possible), duration in seconds and gain.

MNE Scan is MNE-CPP's real-time data acquisition and processing application. It uses a modular plugin pipeline where data flows from acquisition plugins through processing stages to output plugins. Users wire plugins together in a visual GUI, enabling flexible experiment setups without writing code.

Real-time acquisition from MEG and EEG hardware (BabyMEG, Neuromag/Elekta/MEGIN, BrainAmp, gUSBamp, EEGoSports, TMSI, Natus) or via generic protocols (FieldTrip Buffer, Lab Streaming Layer) Signal processing including real-time filtering, noise reduction (SSP/compensators), signal-space separation, and artifact rejection Real-time averaging with configurable baseline correction and artifact thresholds Forward modeling with on-the-fly BEM-based computation and optional HPI-driven head-position updates Source localization using minimum-norm estimates (MNE), including real-time cortical source mapping with 3D visualization Head position monitoring with continuous HPI coil fitting for MEG systems Neuronal connectivity estimation in real time File recording in FIFF format for offline analysis Pre-recorded data playback via the FiffSimulator plugin for testing and development

MNE Scan plugins fall into three categories: Category Role Examples Sensor Acquire data from hardware or network streams FiffSimulator, BabyMEG, BrainAmp, LSL, FieldTrip Buffer Algorithm Process data in the pipeline Averaging, Covariance, Noise Reduction, Forward Solution, MNE, HPI IO Output or store results Write-to-File Plugins are loaded as shared libraries at runtime and communicate through typed input/output connectors linked by lock-free ring buffers.
Below are guides to get you started with MNE Scan.

The Signal-Space Projection (SSP) is one approach to rejection of external disturbances in software. This section presents the relevant mathematical details of this method. Method · API · Example Signal-space projection (SSP) Suppression of environmental and physiological artifacts by projecting the data onto the complement of a noise subspace. Understand the method Signal-Space Projection Signal-Space Projection › Estimation of the Noise Subspace Command-line tools mne_cov2proj Use the API FiffProj FiffInfo::make_projector() Run an example Read a segment of raw dataStart here Tour of the FIFF data structures Fit continuous HPI coils

Unlike many other noise-cancellation approaches, SSP does not require additional reference sensors to record the disturbance fields. Instead, SSP relies on the fact that the magnetic field distributions generated by the sources in the brain have spatial distributions sufficiently different from those generated by external noise sources. Furthermore, it is implicitly assumed that the linear space spanned by the significant external noise patterns has a low dimension. Without loss of generality we can always decompose any nnn-channel measurement b(t)b(t)b(t) into its signal and noise components as: b(t)=bs(t)+bn(t)b(t) = b_s(t) + b_n(t)b(t)=bs​(t)+bn​(t) Further, if we know that bn(t)b_n(t)bn​(t) is well characterized by a few field patterns b1…bmb_1 \ldots b_mb1​…bm​, we can express the disturbance as: bn(t)=Ucn(t)+e(t)b_n(t) = Uc_n(t) + e(t)bn​(t)=Ucn​(t)+e(t) where the columns of UUU constitute an orthonormal basis for b1…bmb_1 \ldots b_mb1​…bm​, cn(t)c_n(t)cn​(t) is an mmm-component column vector, and the error term e(t)e(t)e(t) is small and does not exhibit any consistent spatial distributions over time, i.e., Ce=E{ee⊤}=IC_e = E\{ee^\top\} = ICe​=E{ee⊤}=I. We call the column space of UUU the noise subspace. The basic idea of SSP is that we can find a small basis set b1…bmb_1 \ldots b_mb1​…bm​ such that the conditions described above are satisfied. We can now construct the orthogonal complement operator: P⊥=I−UU⊤P_\perp = I - UU^\topP⊥​=I−UU⊤ and apply it to b(t)b(t)b(t) yielding: bs(t)≈P⊥b(t)b_s(t) \approx P_\perp b(t)bs​(t)≈P⊥​b(t) since P⊥bn(t)=P⊥(Ucn(t)+e(t))≈0P_\perp b_n(t) = P_\perp (Uc_n(t) + e(t)) \approx 0P⊥​bn​(t)=P⊥​(Ucn​(t)+e(t))≈0 and P⊥bs(t)≈bs(t)P_\perp b_s(t) \approx b_s(t)P⊥​bs​(t)≈bs​(t). The projection operator P⊥P_\perpP⊥​ is called the signal-space projection operator and generally provides considerable rejection of noise, suppressing external disturbances by a factor of 10 or more.

The effectiveness of SSP depends on two factors: Complete noise characterization: The basis set b1…bmb_1 \ldots b_mb1​…bm​ should be able to characterize the disturbance field patterns completely. If this requirement is not satisfied, some noise will leak through because P⊥bn(t)≠0P_\perp b_n(t) \neq 0P⊥​bn​(t)=0. Orthogonality to signal: The angles between the noise subspace spanned by b1…bmb_1 \ldots b_mb1​…bm​ and the signal vectors bs(t)b_s(t)bs​(t) should be as close to π/2\pi/2π/2 as possible. If any of the brain signal vectors bs(t)b_s(t)bs​(t) is close to the noise subspace, not only the noise but also the signal will be attenuated by the application of P⊥P_\perpP⊥​ and, consequently, there might be little gain in signal-to-noise ratio. important Since the signal-space projection modifies the signal vectors originating in the brain, it is necessary to apply the projection to the forward solution in the course of inverse computations.

Application of SSP requires the estimation of the signal vectors b1…bmb_1 \ldots b_mb1​…bm​ constituting the noise subspace. The most common approach is to: Compute a covariance matrix of empty room data Compute its eigenvalue decomposition Employ the eigenvectors corresponding to the highest eigenvalues as basis for the noise subspace It is also customary to use a separate set of vectors for magnetometers and gradiometers in the Vectorview system. SSP vectors can be computed from raw data using mne_process_raw with the --projon and --proj options. Existing projection files (.fif) can also be loaded and applied during batch processing.

The EEG average reference is the mean signal over all the sensors. It is typical in EEG analysis to subtract the average reference from all the sensor signals b1(t),…,bn(t)b^1(t), \ldots, b^n(t)b1(t),…,bn(t): bsj(t)=bj(t)−1n∑kbk(t)b^j_s(t) = b^j(t) - \frac{1}{n}\sum_k b^k(t)bsj​(t)=bj(t)−n1​k∑​bk(t) where the noise term bnj(t)b^j_n(t)bnj​(t) is given by: bnj(t)=1n∑kbk(t)b^j_n(t) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_k b^k(t)bnj​(t)=n1​k∑​bk(t) Thus, the projector vector P⊥P_\perpP⊥​ will be given by: P⊥=1n[1,1,…,1]P_\perp = \frac{1}{n}[1, 1, \ldots, 1]P⊥​=n1​[1,1,…,1] warning When applying SSP, the signal of interest can also be sometimes removed. Therefore, it's always a good idea to check how much the effect of interest is reduced by applying SSP. SSP might remove both the artifact and the signal of interest.

mne_acq lists, inspects, records and re-publishes acquisition sources from the command line. A source is named by the same URI that the acquisition library (mne::AcqDevice::open) takes, so anything that works in code works here.

mne_acq list [--timeout s] mne_acq info <uri> mne_acq record <uri> <file.fif> [--duration s] mne_acq stream <uri> --lsl [--name n] [--duration s] mne_acq stream <uri> --brainflow-multicast <address:port> [--master-board id] [--duration s] mne_acq view <uri> [--window s] [--duration s] [--screenshot file.png]

Command Description list Prints the registered URI schemes and the sources that answer within --timeout seconds (default 1), each with a URI ready for the other commands info <uri> Opens the source and prints its backend, device and, per stream, the sample format, sampling rate, clock and every channel with its kind and unit record <uri> <file.fif> Records the first stream of the source to a raw FIFF file (split into parts like MNE-Python above 2 GB), with trigger events in the stim channel and as annotations stream <uri> --lsl Publishes the first stream of the source as a Lab Streaming Layer outlet (float32, the stream's name unless --name is given) view <uri> Shows the first stream as live traces in a sweep display: a fixed --window that the newest samples overwrite from left to right at the "now" marker, so the traces stand still; trigger events are marked until they are overwritten. Runs until the window is closed, --duration has passed or the source ends stream <uri> --brainflow-multicast Publishes the first stream in BrainFlow's multicast format, so BrainFlow's STREAMING_BOARD in Python, C#, Julia or Java receives it (see below)

Option Description --timeout <s> Seconds to search for sources (list) --duration <s> Seconds to run (record, stream); 0, the default, runs until the source ends or Ctrl+C --lsl Publish as an LSL outlet (stream) --name <n> Name of the published LSL stream (stream) --brainflow-multicast <address:port> Publish in BrainFlow's multicast format to this group, e.g. 225.1.1.1:6677 (stream) --master-board <id> BrainFlow board whose row layout is sent (stream; default -1, the synthetic board) --window <s> Visible time window of view (default 10) --screenshot <file> PNG of the view window when it closes -h, --help Displays help -v, --version Displays the version

URI Source synthetic://?eeg=32&sfreq=1000 Seeded synthetic oddball session fiff:///data/sample_raw.fif?loop=1&speed=2 Replay of a raw FIFF file, paced in real time lsl://NAME A Lab Streaming Layer stream by name rtserver://127.0.0.1:4217?simfile=/data/run_raw.fif The active connector of an mne_rt_server, here its FIFF file simulator replaying a file on the server's computer brainflow://cyton?serial_port=/dev/ttyUSB0 Any board BrainFlow supports, through an installed BrainFlow 5 (see below) streaming_board://225.1.1.1:6677?board=cyton What a BrainFlow session streams with add_streamer, without BrainFlow (see below) brainflow_file:///data/session.csv?board=cyton A file BrainFlow wrote, replayed without BrainFlow (see below) The vendor amplifiers (eego://, natus://, babymeg://, ...) are listed by mne_acq list, each with its parameters.

brainflow://<board> opens a board through BrainFlow's BoardController library, which is loaded when the source is opened and is never part of MNE-CPP: library= names it, otherwise MNE_CPP_BRAINFLOW_LIB, then the library of pip install brainflow, then the system loader. BrainFlow 5 is required. The board is BrainFlow's id (-1) or name (synthetic, cyton_daisy, CYTON_DAISY_BOARD); the parameters are BrainFlow's input parameters (serial_port, mac_address, ip_address, ip_port, ip_protocol, other_info, timeout, serial_number, file, master_board, ...). Every row of the board becomes a channel in BrainFlow's units: EEG, EMG, ECG and EOG in microvolts (scaled to volts), temperature in degrees Celsius, the timestamp row in seconds since 1970. The timestamp row is the stream's clock, and a nonzero value in the marker row is an event. mne_acq record "brainflow://cyton_daisy?serial_port=/dev/ttyUSB0" session_raw.fif --duration 60 A BrainFlow session in another program or on another computer can stream its board with board.add_streamer("streaming_board://225.1.1.1:6677"). streaming_board:// receives that stream without BrainFlow: the target is the same address and port (a multicast group is joined on the interface of the default route, as BrainFlow's STREAMING_BOARD does), and board= names the board behind the stream, whose row layout is needed to read it. The synthetic board, Cyton, Ganglion and Cyton + Daisy are known without BrainFlow; other boards need it installed. The channels are those of brainflow://, and the sender's markers are events (BrainFlow's own STREAMING_BOARD replaces them with its own). streaming_board://?simulate=1 streams a synthetic session in the board's layout to itself. mne_acq record "streaming_board://225.1.1.1:6677?board=cyton" session_raw.fif --duration 60 Files BrainFlow wrote with its file streamer (add_streamer("file://session.csv:w")) or DataFilter.write_file hold a sample per line, the board's rows separated by tabs. brainflow_file:// replays them without BrainFlow, with the channels of brainflow://, the markers as events and the timestamps as clock; board= names the board that recorded the file. realtime=0 replays as fast as the samples are read, which converts a BrainFlow file to FIFF: mne_acq record "brainflow_file:///data/session.csv?board=cyton&realtime=0" session_raw.fif

BrainFlow's STREAMING_BOARD interprets every packet with the row layout of a master board, so the publisher sends that layout: the source's channels fill the board's EEG rows in order (volts as microvolts, as BrainFlow reports EEG), the package row counts samples modulo 256 and the timestamp row holds Unix time. Channels beyond the board's EEG rows are not sent. The synthetic board, Cyton, Ganglion and Cyton + Daisy are known without BrainFlow; the layouts of other boards come from BrainFlow when it is installed (pip install brainflow, or MNE_CPP_BRAINFLOW_LIB pointing to its BoardController library). STREAMING_BOARD fills the marker row from its own insert_marker(). Both sides must use the same BRAINFLOW_BATCH_SIZE (default 3). from brainflow.board_shim import BoardIds, BoardShim, BrainFlowInputParams params = BrainFlowInputParams() params.ip_address, params.ip_port = "225.1.1.1", 6677 params.master_board = BoardIds.SYNTHETIC_BOARD board = BoardShim(BoardIds.STREAMING_BOARD, params) board.prepare_session() board.start_stream()
Code Meaning 0 Success 1 Usage error (unknown command, missing argument, invalid number) 2 The source could not be opened or read, or the output could not be written

Record 60 s of a synthetic session and check the result in MNE-Python: mne_acq record "synthetic://?eeg=32&sfreq=1000" session_raw.fif --duration 60 python -c "import mne; print(mne.io.read_raw_fif('session_raw.fif'))" Re-publish a recorded file to LSL, e.g. for an LSL-based pipeline or LabRecorder: mne_acq stream "fiff:///data/sample_audvis_raw.fif?loop=1" --lsl --name SampleMEG Watch a FIFF replay live with a 5 s window: mne_acq view "fiff:///data/sample_audvis_raw.fif?loop=1" --window 5 Inspect an LSL stream, then record it: mne_acq list mne_acq info lsl://SampleMEG mne_acq record lsl://SampleMEG sample_copy_raw.fif --duration 30
mne_rt_server serves a source to MNE Scan and other MNE-CPP clients over the FIFF real-time protocol; its FiffSimulator replays files through the same fiff:// source.

mne_add_patch_info adds cortical patch statistics to an existing source space FIFF file. Patch information describes which high-resolution surface vertices are represented by each source space point, enabling more accurate forward and inverse computations. This is a C++ port of the original MNE-C tool by Matti Hämäläinen.
Option Description --src <file> Input source space FIFF file --out <file> Output source space FIFF file with patch info --help Print help --version Print version

When a decimated source space is created (e.g., with mne_make_source_space), each source point represents a patch of the high-resolution cortical surface. This tool computes and stores the mapping between the high-resolution surface vertices and their nearest source space points, along with patch areas. This information is used by the forward solver to improve the accuracy of the lead field computation by properly distributing the source current over each patch rather than treating it as a point source.

Run this tool after creating a source space with mne_make_source_space and before computing the forward solution with mne_forward_solution: Create source space → mne_make_source_space Add patch info → mne_add_patch_info Compute forward solution → mne_forward_solution
# Add patch information to a source space mne_add_patch_info --src sam-oct-6-src.fif --out sam-oct-6-src-patch.fif
mne_add_to_meas_info adds tags from one FIFF file to the measurement info block of another FIFF file. This is a C++ port of the original MNE-C tool by Matti Hämäläinen.
Option Description --add <name> FIFF file containing the tags to add (required) --dest <name> Destination FIFF file to receive the additional tags (required) --help Print help --version Print version

This utility reads all tags from a source FIFF file and appends them to the measurement info block of a destination FIFF file. This is useful for adding metadata (e.g., digitization points, coordinate transforms) to an existing measurement file.

mne_add_triggers adds trigger events to a raw data file's stimulus (STI) channel. It reads a trigger file with sample–value pairs and writes the events into the STI channel of the raw data. The tool prefers STI 014 but falls back to the first available stimulus channel. This is a C++ port of the original MNE-C tool by Matti Hämäläinen.
Option Description --raw <file> Input raw FIFF file --trg <file> Trigger file (sample event_value per line) --out <file> Output FIFF file --help Print help --version Print version
One trigger event per line with sample number and event value separated by whitespace. Lines starting with # are comments. # sample event_value 1000 1 2500 2 4000 1
mne_fix_stim14 — Fix STI 014 by combining STI 001-006 mne_toggle_skips — Toggle skip tags in raw data

mne_annot2labels converts FreeSurfer annotation files (.annot) into individual label files. Each parcellation region in the annotation is written as a separate label file, suitable for use with MNE source space analysis and ROI-based workflows. This is a C++ port of the original MNE-C tool by Matti Hämäläinen.

Option Description --subject <name> Subject name --subjects_dir <dir> Subjects directory (default: $SUBJECTS_DIR) --annot <name> Annotation name (e.g., aparc, aparc.a2009s) --hemi <hemi> Hemisphere: lh or rh (default: both) --outdir <dir> Output directory for label files (default: subject's label/) --surf <name> Surface to use for coordinates (default: white) --help Print help --version Print version

FreeSurfer stores cortical parcellation information in binary annotation files. This tool reads those files and produces one label file per parcellation region. The label files contain vertex indices and their coordinates, which can be used for source-space ROI analysis.

This tool is typically used after FreeSurfer's recon-all has completed, when you need individual label files for source localization analysis. The resulting labels can be used with mne_compute_mne or mne_compute_raw_inverse to extract time courses from specific cortical regions.

# Convert the aparc parcellation to label files for both hemispheres mne_annot2labels --subject sam --annot aparc # Convert only the left hemisphere of aparc.a2009s mne_annot2labels --subject sam --annot aparc.a2009s --hemi lh --outdir ./labels

This page describes the application MNE Anonymize, i.e. mne_anonymize. This application substitutes different Personal Health Information (PHI) and Personal Identifiable Information (PII) fields from a FIFF (Functional Imaging File Format) file (.fif), with other values. De-identifying vs Anonymizing​ PHI or PII can be substituted with default or user-specified values. This way, it is up to the user to have the output file, either anonymized or de-identified. The difference is that a de-identified file can be re-identified back while an anonymized one cannot. For instance, a field included as PHI could be the measurment date and time (see the following paragraph for more information). With MNE Anonymize application, the measurement date and time inside a FiFF file can be either substituted with a default date or it can be modified by a number of days offset. This way, you could de-identify this field in each file within a database of FIFF files and you could then distribute the files for research purposes. At any given time, knowing the number of days to offset the measurement date, a file can be re-identified. (Note. This is just an example, typically .fif files carry a lot more protected information apart from the measurement date).

The GUI is a separate application, mne_anonymize_gui. It accepts the same options to pre-fill its fields, e.g. mne_anonymize_gui --in example.fif -bdf. mne_anonymize always runs on the command line. Both recognize the options below.

MNE Anonymize can also be executed in command line mode. This is intended for users that might want to anonymize a considerable number of files. The following table shows all valid command line options.

Option Description -h --help Displays help on the command line. --no-gui Accepted for compatibility; has no effect. --version Show the version of this appliation. -i --in <infile> File to anonymize. -o --out <outfile> optional Output file <outfile>. As default '_anonymized.fif' is attached to the file name. -v --verbose optional Prints out all the information about each specific anonymized field. Default: false -s --silent optional Prints no output to the terminal, other than interaction with the user or execution errors. -d --delete_input_file_after optional Delete input fiff file after anonymization. A confirmation message will be prompted to the user. Default: false -f --avoid_delete_confirmation optional Avoid confirming the deletion of the input fiff file. Default: false -b --brute optional Also anonymize subject's weight, height, sex and handedness, and project's ID, name, aim and comment. Default: false --md --measurement_date <value> optional Specify the measurement date. Only when anonymizing a single file. Format: DDMMYYYY Default: 01012000. --mdo --measurement_date_offset <value> optional Specify number of days to subtract to the measurement date. Only allowed when anonymizing a single file. Default: 0 --sb --subject_birthday <value> optional Specify the subject's birthday date. Only allowed when anonymizing a single file. Format: DDMMYYYY. Default: 01012000 --sbo --subject_birthday_offset <value> optional Specify number of days to subtract to the subject's birthday. Only allowed when anonymizing a single file. Default: 0 --his <value> optional Specify a Subject's ID within the Hospital system. Only allowed when anonymizing a single file. Default: 'mne_anonymize' --mne_environment optional Also anonymize information added to the fif file through MNE Toolbox, like Working Directory or Command used. Default: false

It is important to remark that tags will not be deleted. The information in the tag will be substituted by other information, either specified by the user or defined in the application by default. This utility modifies the following tags from the fiff file: Tag Description Default Anonymization Value FIFF_FILE_ID, FIFF_BLOCK_ID, FIFF_PARENT_FILE_ID, FIFF_PARENT_BLOCK_ID, FIFF_REF_FILE_ID, FIFF_REF_BLOCK_ID The ID tag includes a measurement date and unique machine ID. The machine ID usually contains the hardware address of the primary LAN card. 2000/01/01 and 00:00:00:00:00:00:00:00 FIFF_MEAS_DATE The date of the measurement. 2000/01/01 FIFF_COMMENT in the measurement block Holds a (textual) description of the acquisition system. 'mne_anonymize' FIFF_EXPERIMENTER The experimenter's name. 'mne_anonymize' FIFF_SUBJ_ID The Subject ID. 0 FIFF_SUBJ_FIRST_NAME The first name of the subject. 'mne_anonymize' FIFF_SUBJ_MIDDLE_NAME The middle name of the subject. 'mne' FIFF_SUBJ_LAST_NAME The last name of the subject. 'mne_anonymize' FIFF_SUBJ_BIRTH_DAY The birthday of the subject. 2000/01/01 FIFF_SUBJ_SEX The sex of the subject. 0 brute mode only FIFF_SUBJ_HAND The handnes of the subject. 0 brute mode only FIFF_SUBJ_WEIGHT The weight of the subject. 0 brute mode only FIFF_SUBJ_HEIGHT The height of the subject. 0 brute mode only FIFF_SUBJ_COMMENT Comment about the subject. 2000/01/01 FIFF_SUBJ_HIS_ID The subject's ID used in the Hospital Information System. 'mne_anonymize' FIFF_PROJ_ID The project ID. 0 brute mode only FIFF_PROJ_NAME The project name. 'mne_anonymize' brute mode only FIFF_PROJ_AIM The project aim. 'mne_anonymize' brute mode only FIFF_PROJ_PERSONS Persons participating in the project. 'mne_anonymize' FIFF_PROJ_COMMENT Comment about the project 'mne_anonymize' brute mode only FIFF_MNE_ENV_WORKING_DIR Working directory where the file was created. 'mne_anonymize' mne_environment or brute mode only FIFF_MNE_ENV_COMMAND_LINE The command used to create the file. 'mne_anonymize' mne_environment or brute mode only | Please note: MNE Anonymize can also alter the measurement date or the subject's birthday date, by offsetting it some number of days before or after the date which is stored in the input file. | | Please note: MNE Anonymize substitutes the information in the FIFF_SUBJ_HIS_ID tag because some laboratories use that field to store other subject specific information. If the --his option is used on the command line, followed by some text, the FIFF_SUBJ_HIS_ID tag will be substituted with the text specified. | | Please note: In case the input fiff file contains MRI data, beware that a subject's face can be reconstructed from it. The current implementation of MNE Anonymize can not anonymize MRI data. |

For all examples we will use MNE-CPP's sample data which can be found inside the project folder in resources/data/MNE-sample-data/MEG/sample folder. If you find that folder empty, please read README.md file inside MNE-sample-data folder. Run mne_anonymize_gui to use the GUI, or mne_anonymize on the command line. For instance: For specifying an input file to anonymize: mne_anonymize --in ../resources/data/MNE-sample-data/MEG/sample/sample_audvis_raw.fif If you are concerned with the space in your drive, you can delete the input file immediately after anonymization through the option --delete_input_file. By default, before file deletion the user will be prompted to confirm the deletion of the input file: mne_anonymize --in ../resources/data/MNE-sample-data/MEG/sample/sample_audvis_raw.fif --delete_input_file You can avoid confirming the deletion with the flag --avoid_delete_confirmation: mne_anonymize --in ../resources/data/MNE-sample-data/MEG/sample/sample_audvis_raw.fif --delete_input_file --avoid_delete_confirmation If you specify the input and the output files with the same name, by default the application will ask you to confirm deletion of the input file. You can also avoid the confirmation and force the deletion with the option --avoid_delete_confirmation. mne_anonymize --in ../resources/data/MNE-sample-data/MEG/sample/sample_audvis_raw.fif --out ../resources/data/MNE-sample-data/MEG/sample/sample_audvis_raw.fif --delete_input_file --avoid_delete_confirmation In order to substract 35 days from all measurement dates, both in the ID and FIFF_MEAS_DATE tags, use: mne_anonymize --in ../resources/data/MNE-sample-data/MEG/sample/sample_audvis_raw.fif --measurement_date_offset 35 Typical use with abbreviated options. This command will call mne_anonymize, specify the input file, set verbose mode and brute mode on. It will also set delete_input_file on, avoiding the deletion confirmation, and finally set the measurement date to be 35 days before the date registered in the file. mne_anonymize -i ../resources/data/MNE-sample-data/MEG/sample/sample_audvis_raw.fif -vbdf --mdo 35

Fiff files may include Personal Health Information and Personal Identifyable information. The consequences of openly distributing this kind of protected information can be dire. Typically, the regulatory bodies in charge of these issues in each state or country will describe methods for deidentify and anonymize data. In the United States of America, the law related to this problem is the well-known HIPAA, issued by the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). This law mentions two main ways to know when it is OK to distribute a file with patient information in it more info here. MNE Anonymize is designed to implement the "safe harbor" approach, by which if the data is stripped from the following info, it is then considered "safe": Names All geographic subdivisions smaller than a state, including street address, city, county, precinct, ZIP code, and their equivalent geocodes, except for the initial three digits of the ZIP code if, according to the current publicly available data from the Bureau of the Census: All elements of dates (except year) for dates that are directly related to an individual, including birth date, admission date, discharge date, death date, and all ages over 89 and all elements of dates (including year) indicative of such age, except that such ages and elements may be aggregated into a single category of age 90 or older Telephone numbers Vehicle identifiers and serial numbers, including license plate numbers Fax numbers Device identifiers and serial numbers Email addresses Web Universal Resource Locators (URLs) Social security numbers Internet Protocol (IP) addresses Medical record numbers Biometric identifiers, including finger and voice prints Health plan beneficiary numbers Full-face photographs and any comparable images Account numbers Any other unique identifying number, characteristic, or code, except for specific codes/names assigned to a certain file which could allow to re-identify the file. For instance, a new research-oriented id# asigned to a specific subject. There are two requirements for this exception: (1) this new code/number must not be derived from the actual data, and (2) the actual relational table between each code and the protected information cannot be disclosed. Certificate/license numbers Depending on the settings during acquisition the FIFF files may contain few or many of the previous fields, stored in plain text, i.e., in unencrypted form.

An initial approach to deal with sensible information in a file would be to just delete it or maybe alter it "in-place", like other applications do. However, we think this is not a good idea. Firstly, some of these fields, like Subject Name or Measuremenet date, are needed and expected by other software packages, to simply delete them might cause some trouble later. Moreover, it doesn't seem to be a neat job to alter the actual information by masking it with a default character set, e.g., substituing the name Peter C Smith with xxxxx x xxxxx. Some of the fields of data in a FIFF file are quite long, and an individual subject might have a particularly long name. Therefore, a subject might not be properly de-identified or anonymized if we were to follow this route. But most importantly, we consider that the best way to modify the information in a FIFF file is to recompute completely the actual information and the structure it is stored in. Since the FIFF format implies a linked list of tags with information in them, MNE Anonymize will follow this list of tags from the begining until the end, while creating a new tag with anonymized or de-identified information wherever needed. This way, "hidden tags" or unlinked tags in the input file will not be copied to the output. The so-called free list of tags, will not be copied to the output anonymized file either. The tag directory will not be copied to the output file either. This implies that the actual final size of the output file will slightly differ from the input file. If a specific tag with PHI or PII infomation is not present in the FIFF file, mne_anonymize will not create it. MNE Anonymize does not modify the input file. Moreover, this application can even read from write-protected folders. The new/altered output information will be stored in a newly created FIFF file. However, depending on the options, after MNE Anonymize has processed a FIFF file, there might be no way to recover the original information. Use this application with caution.

An experimental WebAssembly build of MNE Anonymize is available. It runs entirely locally inside the browser — no installation needed, no data uploaded. Load a FIFF file, anonymize it, and download the result — all without any data leaving your machine. Learn more about data privacy.
